blocks.text: For centuries many Turkmen families moved with their flocks between pastures, and they lived in a round felt tent that could be taken down and carried on camels. English calls it a yurt. Turkmen calls it *öý*, the same word as **house** and **home**, or *ak öý*, **white house**, after its white felt. When years of smoke from the hearth have darkened the felt and the wood, it becomes a *gara öý*, a **black house**.

The frame has three main parts. The *tärim* is the wall: sections of wooden lattice that fold up for travel and open out like a fan. The *uk* are the long, thin roof poles, bent at the lower end and tied with a woollen rope to the top of the lattice. At the top they all meet the *tüýnük*, a wooden ring that lets the smoke of the hearth out and the daylight in. Reed mats (*gamyş*) go around the lattice, and felt (*keçe*), made from sheep's wool, covers the whole frame. Making and cutting the felt was traditionally women's work.

blocks.tk: Tüýnük uga söýenýär, uklar tärime söýenýär, tärimler bir-birine söýenýär.
blocks.en: The ring leans on the poles, the poles lean on the lattice, and the lattices lean on each other.
blocks.source: A Turkmen saying about the parts of the ak öý, as written down in the folk text «Altmyş başly ak öýüm»

blocks.text: To put one up, the door frame goes up first and the lattice sections are tied to it in a circle. Then the ring is lifted and the roof poles are fitted between the ring and the lattice, a job for about four people working together, according to a study of Turkmen tents by Abdurrahman Deveci. Then come the felts. A folk description counts sixty roof poles for a yurt of four lattice sections and ninety for one of six, which is why songs and sayings speak of the *altmyş başly ak öý*, the **sixty-headed white house**.

A new white yurt was the place for guests and for a newly married couple, and a son who married often received his own beside his parents'. Today most Turkmen families live in houses and flats, but the ak öý has not disappeared. Yurts still go up in villages and on summer pastures, at weddings and celebrations, and as cafés and museums of national culture.

blocks.title: One word for home
blocks.text: Because *öý* means any home, *öýde* is **at home** whether the home is a yurt or a flat. And now you can say whose it is: *atamyň öýi*, my grandfather's house, *atamyň öýünde*, at my grandfather's.
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Bu Merdanyň atasynyň ak öýi. Öýüň gapysy gyzyl, keçesi ak. Atasynyň öýünde owadan haly bar. Merdan we jigisi atasyna kömek edýärler.
blocks.en: This is the white yurt of Merdan's grandfather. The door of the house is red, and its felt is white. In his grandfather's home there is a beautiful carpet. Merdan and his younger brother are helping their grandfather.
